interactions.summary: A student reads the Fra Alberigo and Branca d'Oria passage in which traitors to guests fall into hell before bodily death and leave demons occupying their bodies on earth.
Jiang explains that traitors to guests are such extreme offenders that their souls descend immediately to the frozen ninth circle while demons animate their bodies above.
Jiang asks whether demonic or energetic possession is real, and a student answers that in Southeast Asia and Africa such forces are treated as obvious cultural realities.

speaker_notes.note: ASR renders Dante as 'Donnie' in places, but the referent is clearly Dante and the Commedia's logic of premature damnation.

claims.claim: Jiang says betrayal of guests violates hospitality so radically that the traitor's soul is sent to the ninth circle before bodily death.
Jiang says Dante presents Branca d'Oria as still outwardly alive because a demon has taken over the body while the soul is already in hell.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture claim dated 2026-06-24 about Dante's narrative logic.

claims.claim: Jiang treats cross-cultural belief in voodoo, ghosts, and demons as live evidence that possession remains intelligible outside a modern secular frame.

signature_moments.moment: A traitor can keep walking around in public while already having lost the soul and yielded the body to a demon.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a demon took over his body
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the lecture's sharpest images of sin as possession rather than mere moral bookkeeping.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The sacred protection extended to guests, whose betrayal marks the worst zone of treachery in this packet.
The example of a living person whose body appears active on earth while the soul is already frozen in hell.

chronology_notes.note: This packet pushes the lecture from treachery as frozen revenge into treachery as full dispossession, where the soul's fall can precede biological death.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's Southeast Asia example is conversational and culturally broad; the semantic pass preserves it as evidence of lived belief rather than as a precise anthropology claim.
